lesson.title: Sending a Value Back: The return Statement
lesson.summary: The return statement immediately ends a function call and hands a value back to whatever expression called it, which is how a function delivers a result rather than just performing actions.
lesson.body:
A function's body can contain any statements you like, but the return statement plays a special role: the moment Python executes a return, the function stops running immediately, no matter what statements come after it in the body, and control passes back to wherever the function was called, carrying along whichever value followed the word return. This is different from every other statement you have written so far, since an if statement or a loop lets execution continue to the next line when it finishes, but return does not; it exits the function outright, even if there are ten more lines of code sitting below it that never get a chance to run.

This immediate exit is genuinely useful, not just a quirk to watch out for. Consider:

def classify(n):
    if n < 0:
        return "negative"
    if n == 0:
        return "zero"
    return "positive"

Tracing classify(-5): the first condition, -5 < 0, is True, so Python executes return "negative" right there, and the function ends immediately. The line if n == 0 is never reached, and neither is the final return "positive", because the first return already handed control back out. Tracing classify(0): -5 < 0 is now 0 < 0, which is False, so the function moves past the first if. Then n == 0 checks 0 == 0, which is True, so return "zero" runs and the function exits at that point. Tracing classify(7): both earlier conditions are False, so execution falls all the way through to the final return "positive", the only line left to run.

It is important to understand what happens when a function has no return statement, or reaches the end of its body without hitting one. In that case, Python does not leave the caller with nothing; it automatically supplies the special value None as the result. This trips up beginners who write a function that prints something, expecting the print to count as the function's output. def show_double(n): print(n * 2) does display a number on the screen when called, but show_double(5) itself evaluates to None, not 10, because printing is an action taken during the function's execution, while returning is the separate, explicit act of handing a value back to the caller. Writing result = show_double(5) leaves result bound to None, which is rarely what a beginner intended.

Because return exits as soon as it runs, it also gives you a clean way to handle special cases at the top of a function before the main logic even begins. A function that starts with if not isinstance(value, (int, float)): return None immediately hands back None for invalid input and never executes the rest of the body at all, which is a much clearer way to guard against bad input than wrapping the entire remaining body in a large if-else block.

This pattern, sometimes called an early return or a guard clause, tends to produce flatter, more readable functions than nesting every case inside one giant if-elif-else chain. It also matters that return can appear more than once in a function, as classify shows with its three separate return statements, and that this is completely different from a function that only ever reaches one return at the very end. Both styles are valid Python, but recognizing that only one return statement actually executes on any given call, whichever one Python's flow of control happens to reach first, is essential for tracing what a function will do before you run it.
